*Question from gemini: How do systemic vascular and metabolic risk indicators—such as history of coronary heart disease, diabetes, and blood pressure—correlate with neurological markers of brain damage, specifically brain tissue atrophy and brain infarct volume? (delete later)*

Load libraries

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(ggplot2)
```

Load the clean and augmented data

```{r}
clean_data <- read_tsv(file = "../data/03_dat_aug.tsv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

Create new subset `cor_data` with selected variables associated with cardiovascular and brain health

```{r}
cor_data <- clean_data |> 
  select("atrophy", #brain 
         "numinf",  #brain 
         "stroke",  #brain 
         "volinf",  #brain
         "whgrd",   #brain
         "dsst",    #brain
         "chf",     #cd ~ cardiovascular
         "chd",     #cd
         "sbp",     #cd
         "ldl",     #cd
         "diabetes",#cd
         "plt",     #cd
         "aai")     #cd
```

Investigate the subset

```{r}
cor_data |> 
  str() 
```

Prepare the data set for correlation analysis: The variables `stroke` and `chd` are ordinal, including 3 categories (0,1,2). We split the initial variables into 2 new ones:

-stroke -\> stroke_tia (tia: transient ischemic attack), stroke_event

-chd -\> chd-angina, chd_mi (mi: myocardial infarction) (abbreviations from rigr package documentation)

```{r}
cor_data <- cor_data |>
  mutate(stroke_tia = case_when(stroke == 1 ~ 1,
                                  .default = 0),
         stroke_event = case_when(stroke == 2 ~ 1,
                                  .default = 0),
         chd_angina = case_when(chd == 1 ~ 1,
                                  .default = 0),
         chd_mi = case_when(chd == 2 ~ 1,
                                  .default = 0)) |>
  select(-stroke,
         -chd)
```

Check normality of numeric (continuous, discrete) variables to choose the correlation method.

```{r}
cor_data |> 
  select("numinf",
         "volinf",
         "dsst",
         "sbp",
         "ldl",
         "plt",
         "aai") |> 
  map(shapiro.test)
```

The variables in the subset are classified as binary, ordinal, discrete or continuous and the majority of the numeric ones are not normally distributed (p-value\<0.05), for this reason we choose the Spearman correlation method.

Study the correlation between the variables associated with brain and cardiovascular health

```{r}
# correlation matrix
 cardio_vars <- cor_data |> 
   select(dsst, # continuous
         atrophy, # ordinal 
         whgrd, # ordinal
         numinf, # discrete
         volinf, # continuous
         stroke_tia, # binary
         stroke_event) # binary 
 brain_vars <- cor_data |> 
   select(sbp, # continuous
         ldl, # continuous
         aai, # continuous
         chf, # binary
         diabetes, # binary
         chd_angina,# binary
         chd_mi, # binary
         plt) # discrete
 
 cor_matrix <- round(cor(cardio_vars,
                         brain_vars,
                         method = "spearman"),
                     5)
```

Investigate correlation matrix

```{r}
cor_matrix |> 
 range()
```

Tidy the data before visualization

```{r}
cor_tbl <- cor_matrix |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "brain") |> 
  pivot_longer(cols = -brain,
               names_to = "cardiovascular",
               values_to = "correlation")
```

Create a heatmap to visualize the results from the correlation matrix

```{r}
cor_heatmap <- cor_tbl |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = brain,
             y = cardiovascular,
             fill = correlation)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "darkolivegreen",
                       mid = "white",
                       high = "darkmagenta",
                       midpoint = 0,
                       limits = c(-0.35,0.35)) +
  labs(title = "Correlation between brain and cardiovascular variables",
       x = "Brain variables",
       y = "Cardiovascular variables",
       fill = "Spearman correlation",
       caption = "Note: Color scale limited to [-0.35, 0.35] to improve visual contrast.")+
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5,
                                  margin = margin(b = 15), # b ~ bottom
                                  size = 13),
        axis.title.x = element_text(margin = margin(t = 15)), # t ~ top
        axis.title.y = element_text(margin = margin(r = 15)),
    legend.position = "bottom")

cor_heatmap

ggsave("../results/08_analysis_4/correlation_heatmap.png",
       cor_heatmap,
       width = 8,
       height = 6,
       bg = "white",
       dpi = 300)
```

The heatmap shows that the correlations between the two sets of variables are weak, as their values have a range of -0.16570 - 0.20605 and the correlation is stronger when the value is closer to +/- 1.

The strongest positive correlation in this analysis, is between `dsst` (Digit Symbol Substitution Test score) and `aai` (Ankle Brachial Index). Ankle Brachial Index reflects overall vascular health and blood flow, while the Digit Symbol Substitution score is a neurophychological test used to assess cognitive performance. Therefore, a normal aai (1.0-1.4) indicates good circulation which helps maintain healthy blood flow to the brain and supports better cognitive processing on the dsst (higher score). This connection between blood flow and brain function could explain why the two variables show a positive correlation. Furthermore, `aai` shows negative correlation with the other brain variables (`numinf`, `volinf`, `stroke_event` and `whgrd`). Since a lower `aai` indicates poorer circulation, worse vascular health would go with a higher number and volume of infarcts and more white-matter damage (`whgrd`). In contrast, `sbp` (Systolic Blood Pressure) shows the strongest negative correlation with `dsst` and positive with the rest of the brain markers.

Diabetes and cardiovascular risk indicators (`chf`, `chd_mi`, `chd_angina`) show positive correlations with `stroke_event` and `volinf`. All of these conditions can damage blood vessels and affect the blood flow to the brain, which could explain the association.

Finally, `atrophy` , `stroke_tia`, `plt` and `ldl` show the weakest correlations (values closer to 0).

Next, we focused our exploratory analysis on binary variables, since a correlation coefficient provides only a limited understanding between them. More specifically, we selected the vascular and metabolic risk indicators in relation to `stroke_event` to compare the percentage of people with and without each condition who had a stroke event.

```{r}
bar_plot <- cor_data |> 
  select(chf, 
         diabetes, 
         chd_angina, 
         chd_mi, 
         stroke_event) |> 
  pivot_longer(cols = -stroke_event,
               names_to = "cardio_var",
               values_to = "condition") |> 
  group_by(cardio_var, 
           condition) |> 
  summarise(stroke_rate = mean(stroke_event),
            .groups = "drop")|>
  mutate(stroke_per = round(stroke_rate * 100)) |> 
  
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(condition), # with factor() ggplot recognises the categorical variable
             y = stroke_rate,
             fill = cardio_var)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = str_c(stroke_per, 
                              "%")),
                position = position_dodge(0.9),
                vjust = -0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ cardio_var, 
             nrow = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0,0.3)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("chf" = "#9BCD9B",
                               "diabetes" = "#8B3A62",
                               "chd_angina" = "#CDCD00",
                               "chd_mi" = "#8B8B7A")) +
  labs(title = "Stroke event rate by cardiovascular condition",
       x = "Condition (0 = absent, 1 = present)",
       y = "Stroke event rate") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5,
                                  margin = margin(b = 20), # b ~ bottom
                                  size = 13),
        axis.title.x = element_text(margin = margin(t = 20)),# t ~ top
        axis.title.y = element_text(margin = margin(r = 20)),
        legend.position = "none")

bar_plot

ggsave("../results/08_analysis_4/stroke_event_rate_by_cd_condition.png",
       bar_plot,
       width = 8,
       height = 6,
       bg = "white",
       dpi = 300)
```

In the bar plot a higher stroke percentage was represented by people with a cardiovascular condition (coded 1) than people without it (coded 0), indicating that cardiac factors can influence the stroke outcome. The stroke percentage was about 8-9% in people without a condition and about 18-26% in people with one, with `chf` representing the highest rate. This suggests that cardiac and metabolic conditions may be associated with a higher chance of having a stroke, which also agrees with the postive correlations in the heatmap. However, the goal of this analysis was to explore possible correlations between variables and not building a model to predict a stroke event. Finally, the percentages are not very precise as the groups of people with a condition are small and the same people can have several conditions.
